item.title: FRAGILE: off-pump vs on-pump CABG in prefrail and frail patients, 10.9% vs 16.0% 30-day events, not significant
item.description:
Circulation · RCT · 2026-11-10

A multicentre, open-label Brazilian-led trial randomized 508 prefrail or frail patients aged 60 or older to off-pump or on-pump CABG. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, MI, stroke, renal failure, ARDS or reoperation for bleeding.

Take-home

  • The 30-day composite occurred in 10.9% with off-pump and 16.0% with on-pump CABG (relative risk 1.47, 95% CI 0.94 to 2.31; P=0.09)
  • Surgical wound infection at 30 days was more frequent with on-pump surgery: 8.0% vs 3.5% (P=0.04)
  • No significant differences in neurocognitive or quality-of-life outcomes at 1 year; estimated 1-year survival 96.1% vs 92.8% (P=0.099)

Why it matters. Off-pump versus on-pump CABG is one of the longest-running arguments in cardiac surgery, and frail older patients are where proponents of avoiding bypass make their strongest case. FRAGILE is a randomized test in exactly that group.

What they did. Patients aged 60 or older classified as prefrail or frail and scheduled for CABG were randomized 1:1 between January 2018 and December 2024 to off-pump (n=258) or on-pump (n=250) surgery. The trial was multicentre and open-label. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, ARDS or reoperation for bleeding. Analysis was by intention to treat.

What they found.

  • Primary composite: 28 patients (10.9%) off-pump vs 40 (16.0%) on-pump; relative risk 1.47 (0.94 to 2.31), P=0.09.
  • Wound infection at 30 days: 3.5% off-pump vs 8.0% on-pump (P=0.04).
  • Estimated 1-year survival 96.1% vs 92.8% (P=0.099).
  • No significant differences in neurocognitive or quality-of-life outcomes at 1 year.

Caveats. The main comparison missed significance, so this is a trial of similar outcomes with a trend, not proof of benefit. Open-label design. The wound infection finding is a secondary outcome. The registered primary outcome on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02338947) matches the one reported.

For the anesthesiologist. Do not read this as a reason to steer frail patients toward off-pump surgery for hard outcomes. It does mean that either strategy is defensible, and the team should plan the anesthetic around the surgeon's usual technique, with conversion to bypass and hemodynamic instability during grafting in mind.

item.title: VILARE: videolaryngoscopy raised first-attempt intubation success for anaesthesia residents, 79.2% vs 70.2%
item.description:
Anaesthesia · RCT · 2026-11-09

A pragmatic multicentre trial randomized 1001 adults needing tracheal intubation for surgery to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the first attempt. Every intubation was performed by an anaesthesia resident under consultant supervision.

Take-home

  • First-attempt success was 79.2% with videolaryngoscopy vs 70.2% with direct laryngoscopy (absolute difference 9.0%, 95% CI 3.7 to 14.4)
  • Videolaryngoscopy gave better glottic views, less operator-reported difficulty (33.5% vs 47.2%) and fewer procedural complications (7.7% vs 18.2%)
  • There was no clinically meaningful difference in intubation time or need for adjunct airway devices

Why it matters. Videolaryngoscopy improves the glottic view and first-attempt success, but much of that evidence comes from experienced operators, while most routine intubations in teaching hospitals are done by residents. Multicentre evidence in that group was limited.

What they did. VILARE was a pragmatic multicentre randomized trial run at Spanish hospitals. Adults having surgery that required tracheal intubation were assigned to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the first attempt. All intubations were performed by anaesthesia residents under consultant supervision. The primary outcome was successful intubation on the first attempt.

What they found. 1001 patients were enrolled, 501 to videolaryngoscopy and 500 to direct laryngoscopy.

  • First-attempt success: 79.2% vs 70.2%, absolute difference 9.0% (95% CI 3.7 to 14.4).
  • Modified Cormack-Lehane grade 2 or 2a view: 93.3% vs 80.8%.
  • Operator-reported difficulty: 33.5% vs 47.2%. Procedural complications: 7.7% vs 18.2%.
  • No clinically meaningful difference in intubation time or in the need for adjunct airway devices.

Caveats. The device cannot be hidden from the operator, and difficulty is operator-reported, so the secondary outcomes are softer than the primary one. Participants were adults having surgery, so these results do not speak to emergency or ICU intubation. I could only read the abstract, so the authors' own limitations are not listed.

For the anesthesiologist. For programmes that train residents, this supports videolaryngoscopy as the default first device: about nine more successful first passes per 100 patients and fewer complications without a time penalty. Direct laryngoscopy skills still belong in the curriculum, because devices fail and trainees need to learn both.

item.title: RACE-CARS: a community and EMS bundle did not improve good neurologic survival after cardiac arrest, 9.0% vs 9.4%
item.description:
NEJM · RCT · 2026-11-08

This registry-based cluster-randomized trial in North Carolina counties tested a four-part package of telecommunicator training, community CPR training and more early AED use against usual care in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

Take-home

  • Good neurologic survival to discharge was 9.0% with the intervention and 9.4% with usual care (adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.26)
  • The trial included 28 intervention clusters (11,615 patients) and 27 usual-care clusters (10,844 patients) from July 2022 to June 2026
  • A multifaceted community and EMS strategy did not give a greater share of patients a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care

Why it matters. Early CPR, telecommunicator-assisted CPR and public-access defibrillation are the backbone of cardiac arrest survival, and communities are urged to invest in them. Randomized evidence that a bundled community strategy improves outcomes has been lacking, which is what this large trial tested.

What they did. RACE-CARS was a registry-based, cluster-randomized trial in North Carolina. Counties were grouped into clusters and randomized 1:1 to a multifaceted intervention or usual care. The intervention had four parts: training 911 telecommunicators to recognize arrest faster, training them to give CPR instructions to bystanders, community CPR training, and more use of AEDs by first responders or bystanders before EMS arrival. Data came from the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1 or 2).

What they found. From July 2022 to June 2026, 28 clusters (11,615 patients) were assigned to the intervention and 27 clusters (10,844 patients) to usual care. Good neurologic survival was 9.0% (1048 of 11,608) vs 9.4% (1017 of 10,839), adjusted OR 0.97 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.26, P=0.80).

Caveats. The trial tests one bundle against usual care. It says nothing about the value of each component, and a null result does not show that CPR training or AEDs are useless. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04660526) registers the same primary outcome. I could only read the abstract, so the authors' own limitations are not listed.

For the anesthesiologist. Little changes at the bedside: high-quality CPR and early defibrillation remain the standard. For perioperative and ICU physicians who sit on hospital or regional resuscitation committees, the message is that adding training and AED programmes may not be enough on its own to move neurologic survival.

item.title: ON-SCENE: prehospital ECPR was linked to higher survival in refractory arrest at 50 or younger, 40% vs 20%
item.description:
NEJM · Observational · 2026-11-07

A nationwide nonrandomized Dutch study compared young adults with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest attended by helicopter EMS able to start ECPR on scene with those attended by helicopter EMS without that capability.

Take-home

  • Survival to discharge was 40% (57 of 144) with prehospital ECPR vs 20% (17 of 87) with conventional care (OR 2.72, 1.59 to 4.66)
  • Favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months was 36% (51 of 141) vs 13% (11 of 85)
  • There were 32 adverse events in the ECPR group and 11 in the conventional group

Why it matters. Refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in younger adults carries a grim prognosis with conventional resuscitation, and extracorporeal CPR (ECPR) with venoarterial ECMO is increasingly offered in hospital. Data on taking ECPR to the scene were limited for patients aged 50 or younger.

What they did. In a nationwide, nonrandomized study in the Netherlands, 144 adults aged 50 or younger attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR were compared with 87 attended by HEMS without ECPR capability. The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.

What they found.

  • Survival to discharge: 57 of 144 (40%) vs 17 of 87 (20%), odds ratio 2.72 (95% CI 1.59 to 4.66, P=0.002).
  • Favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months: 51 of 141 (36%) vs 11 of 85 (13%).
  • Adverse events: 32 in the ECPR group vs 11 in the conventional group.

Caveats. This was not randomized. Which group a patient fell into depended on the HEMS team that attended, so unmeasured differences can remain, and the findings apply only to carefully selected patients aged 50 or younger. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04620070) registers hospital survival as the primary outcome, matching the paper. I could only read the abstract, so the authors' own limitations are not listed.

For the anesthesiologist. Anesthesiologists are often part of HEMS, ECMO and perfusion teams, so this is an important signal that on-scene cannulation can be done and may help the right patient. It does not replace a randomized trial. Centres building an ECPR pathway should use strict selection criteria, have a dedicated drilled team and a receiving ECMO centre, and track complications from the start.

item.title: ISCHEMIA-EXTEND: routine invasive strategy did not improve 11-year survival in stable coronary disease, 25.8% vs 26.9%
item.description:
JAMA · Trial update · 2026-11-07

Long-term follow-up of the 5,179-participant ISCHEMIA trial, through December 2025, compared an initial invasive strategy (angiography and revascularization plus medical therapy) with initial conservative medical therapy for survival in chronic coronary disease with moderate or severe ischemia.

Take-home

  • At 11 years, all-cause mortality was 25.8% with an initial invasive strategy vs 26.9% with conservative care (adjusted HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.86-1.09).
  • Cardiovascular mortality was 15.8% vs 17.1% (adjusted HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.75-1.02); noncardiovascular mortality was 9.1% vs 8.1% (adjusted HR 1.18, 0.96-1.45).
  • Bayesian analysis gave a low (18%) probability of a survival benefit above 1 percentage point with invasive management.

Why it matters. ISCHEMIA asked whether adding routine angiography and revascularization to guideline-directed medical therapy helps patients with stable coronary disease and moderate or severe ischemia. Survival curves can separate late, so this extension followed participants through December 2025 (median 9 years, up to 13.4).

What they did. The 5,179 participants (median age 64, 23% women, 42% with diabetes, median ejection fraction 60%) had been randomized at 320 sites in 37 countries to an initial invasive strategy or an initial conservative strategy, with invasive care reserved for failure of medical therapy. Analysis was by intention to treat, using Cox and Fine-Gray models, a Bayesian analysis and restricted mean survival time.

What they found. There were 1,071 deaths. At 11 years, all-cause mortality was 25.8% with the invasive strategy and 26.9% with the conservative one (difference -1.0 percentage point, 95% CI -4.2 to 2.1; adjusted HR 0.97). Cardiovascular mortality was 15.8% vs 17.1% (adjusted HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.75-1.02) and noncardiovascular mortality 9.1% vs 8.1% (adjusted HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.96-1.45). The Bayesian probability of a survival benefit larger than 1 percentage point was 18%, and restricted mean survival differed by 14 days (95% CI -41 to 70).

Caveats. Participants had preserved ejection fraction and no left main disease, and people with unacceptable angina or a recent acute coronary syndrome were excluded, so the result does not extend to them. This summary rests on the abstract; the full-text limitations are not listed here.

For the anesthesiologist. Patients with stable ischemic disease who have not been revascularized are not carrying an unaddressed survival penalty. For perioperative planning, the decision to revascularize still rests on symptoms, anatomy and the planned surgery, not on a long-term survival gain from routine invasive management.

item.title: DAPT-SHOCK-AMI: cangrelor inhibited platelets far better than crushed ticagrelor in MI shock, but noninferiority not shown
item.description:
Lancet · RCT · 2026-11-07

A double-blind trial at 29 European hospitals randomized 605 patients with acute MI complicated by cardiogenic shock to intravenous cangrelor or a crushed 180 mg ticagrelor load. It had a laboratory primary endpoint (platelet inhibition at the end of PCI) and a clinical one (death, MI or ischaemic stroke at 30 days).

Take-home

  • Effective platelet inhibition at the end of primary PCI: 100% of 56 with cangrelor vs 22% of 68 with crushed ticagrelor (p<0.0001)
  • Death, MI or ischaemic stroke at 30 days: 38% vs 41%; noninferiority of cangrelor was not demonstrated (difference -4 points, 90% CI -10 to 3)
  • Major bleeding at 30 days was 6% with cangrelor and 5% with ticagrelor; the authors present it as the first P2Y12 trial specific to MI shock

Why it matters. Patients in cardiogenic shock absorb oral drugs poorly: they are intubated, hypoperfused, on opioids and often on ECMO or an Impella. Crushed ticagrelor through a tube is routine, and this is the first randomized look at whether an intravenous P2Y12 inhibitor does better.

What they did. 605 adults with AMI and cardiogenic shock at 29 hospitals in five European countries were randomized double blind to cangrelor (30 μg/kg bolus, 4 μg/kg/min for at least 2 h) or crushed ticagrelor 180 mg. The laboratory endpoint was platelet reactivity index below 50% at the end of PCI; the clinical endpoint, tested for noninferiority with a 1-point margin, was death, MI or ischaemic stroke at 30 days.

What they found.

  • Platelet inhibition: 56/56 (100%) vs 15/68 (22%).
  • Clinical endpoint: 112/298 (38%) vs 126/307 (41%); noninferiority not shown.
  • Major bleeding 6% vs 5%.

Caveats. The laboratory endpoint was measured in only about a fifth of patients. A 1-point noninferiority margin is very tight, so the trial could not show noninferiority despite numerically fewer events with cangrelor; it cannot claim superiority either. A Circulation imaging substudy reports less microvascular obstruction with cangrelor, which the authors call hypothesis-generating.

For the anesthesiologist. In the cath lab or cardiac ICU, assume crushed ticagrelor leaves most shock patients with unreliable platelet inhibition early on. That matters when you are deciding on cannulation, line placement or emergency CABG: an infusion with a short offset may be easier to manage than an oral load whose effect arrives late and lasts days. Bleeding was similar here, but the trial does not settle which strategy improves outcomes.

item.title: OPTIPAM: individualized MAP targets in cardiac surgery stopped early for bleeding (18% vs 3%) with no outcome benefit
item.description:
Anesthesiology · RCT · 2026-11-06

A French multicentre trial randomized elective cardiac surgery patients on bypass to a MAP target within 10% of their preoperative baseline, during surgery and for 24 hours, or to a standard target of 65 mm Hg or more. The primary outcome was death, AKI or neurologic complications at 7 days.

Take-home

  • The trial stopped after 172 patients because the data and safety monitoring board saw more bleeding with individualized MAP
  • Hemorrhagic complications occurred in 18% with individualized MAP vs 3% with standard management (P=0.003)
  • Death, AKI or neurologic complications at 7 days: 32% vs 29% (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.7 to 1.8); benefit could not be determined

Why it matters. Many of us push pressure higher in hypertensive cardiac patients on the theory that their kidneys and brains autoregulate at a higher set point. OPTIPAM is a randomized test of a patient-specific target, and it raises a safety signal nobody was looking for.

What they did. Adults having elective cardiac surgery with CPB at 10 French tertiary centres were randomized, single blind, to a MAP target within ±10% of their preoperative baseline, held through surgery and for 24 hours afterwards, or to MAP of 65 mm Hg or more. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, AKI or prespecified neurologic complications within 7 days.

What they found.

  • The DSMB stopped the trial at 172 patients for excess bleeding in the individualized arm.
  • Intraoperative MAP was higher, 80.6 vs 75.6 mm Hg, but the target was met only 33% of the time, with more vasopressor.
  • Primary outcome 32% vs 29%, RR 1.1 (0.7 to 1.8).
  • Hemorrhagic complications 18% vs 3%.

Caveats. The registration planned 1100 patients, so the efficacy question is unanswered. The separation in pressure was small and adherence was poor. The abstract does not say what the bleeding events were, or whether higher pressure, more vasopressor or chance drove them.

For the anesthesiologist. This does not tell you that 65 mm Hg is enough for everyone, but it is a reason not to chase baseline pressures with vasopressor in the first postoperative day without watching chest tube output. If you target higher pressures after bypass, pair that with a deliberate look at hemostasis and drains. The authors call for future trials to track this bleeding signal.

item.title: TOPIC-2: paravertebral block did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain vs epidural, 22% vs 16% at 6 months
item.description:
BMJ · RCT · 2026-11-05

A UK multicentre open-label trial randomized adults having thoracotomy to paravertebral blockade (three single shots plus a catheter) or a thoracic epidural placed before incision. The primary outcome was chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months.

Take-home

  • Paravertebral blockade did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months: 22% vs 16%, adjusted RR 1.32 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.86)
  • Epidural gave marginally better acute pain on day 1 (worst pain 7.7 mm lower on a 100 mm scale), with no difference on days 2-3
  • Paravertebral had less hypotension (12% vs 18%) and pruritus (4% vs 12%) but more urinary retention (12% vs 6%); the authors say both techniques remain reasonable

Why it matters. Chronic pain after thoracotomy is common and disabling, and the idea that a unilateral paravertebral block might prevent it better than an epidural has driven a lot of practice change. TOPIC-2 is the large pragmatic test of that idea.

What they did. 770 adults at 15 UK thoracic centres were randomized to paravertebral blockade (three single-shot injections before incision, then a paravertebral catheter) or a thoracic epidural loaded before incision. After 33 patients who never had a thoracotomy were excluded, 737 formed the modified intention-to-treat population. Chronic pain meant a worst chest pain score of at least 40 on a 100 mm VAS at six months.

What they found.

  • Chronic pain at six months: 59/272 (22%) paravertebral vs 47/292 (16%) epidural; adjusted RR 1.32 (0.93 to 1.86), P=0.12.
  • Day 1 worst pain 7.7 mm and average pain 7.0 mm higher with paravertebral; no difference on days 2-3.
  • Hypotension 12% vs 18% and pruritus 4% vs 12%, favoring paravertebral; urinary retention 12% vs 6%, favoring epidural.

Caveats. Open label. The six-month primary outcome was available for 564 of 737 patients, and the registry planned 1026 participants, so the trial is smaller than designed. The point estimate leans toward epidural, so the result does not support a preventive benefit of paravertebral block.

For the anesthesiologist. Pick the technique for acute-phase reasons: paravertebral for patients where epidural hypotension, anticoagulation timing or bilateral block worries you; epidural where the best day-1 analgesia matters most. Do not sell either one to patients as a way to prevent chronic pain. The trial is about open thoracotomy, not VATS or robotic resections, where fascial plane blocks dominate.

item.title: LMA instead of tracheal tube for adenotonsillectomy in young children cut respiratory adverse events, 22.5% vs 57.5%
item.description:
BMJ · RCT · 2026-11-04

Four Chinese tertiary hospitals randomized 400 children aged 2 to 6 years having adenotonsillectomy to ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway or an endotracheal tube. The primary outcome was any perioperative respiratory adverse event.

Take-home

  • Perioperative respiratory adverse events occurred in 22.5% with an LMA vs 57.5% with an ETT (risk difference -35.0 points, 95% CI -43.5 to -25.7)
  • The LMA group had less laryngospasm (0% vs 3.0%), desaturation (15.0% vs 28.0%), airway obstruction and severe cough (10.5% vs 42.0%)
  • LMA was converted to ETT in three children, and neither group had serious adverse events; the authors note LMAs were used by experienced anaesthesiologists

Why it matters. Adenotonsillectomy is one of the commonest pediatric anesthetics and one of the most likely to produce laryngospasm and desaturation, especially at emergence. Whether the flexible LMA is safer than intubation has been argued for decades; this is a large multicentre randomized answer.

What they did. 400 children aged 2 to under 7 years (mean 4.7) at four tertiary hospitals were randomized 1:1 to LMA or ETT ventilation for adenotonsillectomy under general anaesthesia. The primary outcome was any perioperative respiratory adverse event: laryngospasm, bronchospasm, desaturation, airway obstruction, severe cough or stridor, analysed by intention to treat.

What they found.

  • Any event: 45/200 (22.5%) vs 115/200 (57.5%).
  • Intraoperative 9.0% vs 17.5%; postoperative 16.5% vs 49.5%, so most of the difference comes after surgery.
  • Severe cough 10.5% vs 42.0%, desaturation 15.0% vs 28.0%, laryngospasm 0% vs 3.0%.
  • Three LMAs converted to ETT; no serious adverse events.

Caveats. The anaesthesiologists were experienced with the LMA in shared-airway surgery, and the surgical team's comfort with it matters too. Allocation could not be blinded, and severe cough is a soft component that drives much of the composite. The trial is registered in the Chinese registry, so it was not checked against ClinicalTrials.gov.

For the anesthesiologist. If your ENT surgeons will work around a flexible LMA, this is strong support for using it in healthy preschool children, particularly for a smoother emergence. Keep the ETT for cases where the airway will be shared poorly, for obstructive apnea severe enough that you want a secured airway, or when the team has little LMA experience.

item.title: IRIS-MAIN: left main PCI and CABG had similar 10-year mortality in a 5,379-patient Asian registry, 24.0% vs 22.9%
item.description:
Lancet · Registry · 2026-11-03

Investigators analysed the prospective IRIS-MAIN registry from 46 hospitals in South Korea, India, Japan, Indonesia and Malaysia, comparing PCI with drug-eluting stents against isolated CABG for unprotected left main disease. They used a target trial emulation framework with propensity-score overlap weighting; median follow-up was 10 years.

Take-home

  • No statistically detectable difference in 10-year all-cause mortality: PCI 24.0% vs CABG 22.9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.87-1.14); p=0.99
  • The authors note the confidence interval does not exclude a mortality benefit or harm with either strategy
  • For patients suitable for either strategy, they suggest multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion to weigh the potential trade-offs

Why it matters. Left main disease is where the heart-team argument gets sharpest, and we anesthetize the patients on both sides of it. Randomized trials follow selected patients; this registry asks the same question in routine practice, with long follow-up.

What they did. IRIS-MAIN enrolled 6,900 adults with unprotected left main stenosis of at least 50% at 46 hospitals in five Asian countries between 2003 and 2024. The analysis covers the 5,379 who had PCI with drug-eluting stents (3,836) or isolated CABG (1,543). The team emulated a target trial and used overlap weighting. All-cause mortality was the primary outcome, which matches the ClinicalTrials.gov registration (death at 10 years).

What they found. Median follow-up was 10.0 years. Weighted 10-year mortality was 24.0% with PCI and 22.9% with CABG (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.14; p=0.99).

Caveats.

  • This is not a randomized comparison. Weighting handles measured covariates only, and who was sent to surgery over 22 years is exactly the kind of choice that weighting can miss.
  • The authors say plainly that this cannot establish equivalence.
  • I read the abstract, which gives no stroke, MI or repeat revascularization figures, so survival is only part of the trade-off.
  • Stents and surgical practice changed a lot across the enrolment period, and the population is Asian.

For us. This changes no anesthetic plan. It does temper any assumption that a left main patient sent for PCI has been given a clearly worse survival outlook, without proving the two are the same. If you sit on a heart team, use it as context for a shared decision, not as a tiebreaker.

item.title: FDA early alert: ButterflyBVM bag-valve-masks can develop bellows holes that leak tidal volume; nine lots being removed
item.description:
FDA · Safety alert · 2026-11-03

Compact Medical is removing some lots of its single-use ButterflyBVM resuscitators and correcting the use instructions for others, because holes in the bellows can let tidal volume leak instead of reaching the patient. FDA posted the early alert on November 3.

Take-home

  • Holes can form in the bellows, causing inadequate ventilation and hypoxia; lots 000109 through 000117 have a higher rate of holes than previously observed
  • Do not use lots 000109-000117: remove them from every location, including crash carts and vehicles, once replacement BVMs are in place
  • For the listed lots 000081-000108, do the Pre-Use Test before every use, keep backup BVMs, and switch immediately if a hole appears

Why it matters. A bag-valve-mask is the device you reach for when everything else has failed, and it usually sits unused on a cart until that moment. A leak you discover during a difficult ventilation is the wrong time to learn about this.

What happened. Compact Medical told customers on September 26 and October 7, and FDA posted the early alert on November 3. Holes can form in the bellows, so tidal volume leaks instead of reaching the patient. Compact Medical had reported no serious injuries or deaths as of November 2.

What is affected.

  • Removal: ButterflyBVM READY (R300, R308) lots 000109-000113 and 000115-000117, and ButterflyBVM (A100, A108) lot 000114.
  • Correction: listed READY, A100/A108 and PLUS (P200, P208) lots between 000081 and 000108. These stay in use with the updated instructions.
  • If packaging and labeling are gone, assume the device is in the affected lots.

What users are told. Secure replacements first so no area is left without a resuscitator. Quarantine removed units and label them DO NOT USE. Run the Pre-Use Test before every use on correction lots. If chest rise is poor or saturation falls, check the back of the device for a hole. If there is one, change to a backup BVM immediately.

For us. Ask your supply chain or anesthesia techs whether your hospital stocks this brand, including transport bags, airway carts and remote sites. Any resuscitator bag should get a quick function check before you depend on it. Ventilation that looks wrong with a good mask seal should prompt you to suspect the device early and swap it.

item.title: Sugammadex vs neostigmine: update of 165 RCTs finds reversal 10.5 min faster and fewer adverse events
item.description:
European Journal of Anaesthesiology · Meta-analysis · 2026-11-03

Putzu and colleagues updated the 2017 Cochrane review comparing sugammadex with neostigmine in adults given rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures. They pooled randomized trials with meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses and GRADE, searching up to December 2025.

Take-home

  • 165 trials, 19 124 participants: sugammadex 2 mg/kg reached TOF above 0.9 from second twitch faster than neostigmine 0.05 mg/kg (MD -10.49 min; moderate)
  • Sugammadex probably reduces patients with at least one adverse event: RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.61-0.84; moderate certainty)
  • It probably reduces residual block, desaturation, atelectasis, airway obstruction and bradycardia; authors say broader use could improve peri-operative outcomes

Why it matters. The argument for neostigmine has been mostly about price. The authors note recent changes in the cost of sugammadex, so the question of whether it should be the routine reversal agent is live again, and 165 trials is a lot of evidence to bring to it.

What they did. This updates a 2017 Cochrane review, with databases searched up to December 2025. Trials enrolled adults receiving rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures. Outcomes were recovery time and adverse events, graded with GRADE and tested with trial sequential analysis.

What they found. Across 19 124 participants, time from second twitch to a TOF ratio above 0.9 was 10.49 minutes shorter (95% CI -11.90 to -9.08) with sugammadex 2 mg/kg than neostigmine 0.05 mg/kg. At least one adverse event: RR 0.72 (0.61-0.84). Residual block, inadequate reversal, desaturation, atelectasis, secretions, airway obstruction, bradycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention were all probably reduced, each at moderate certainty.

Caveats.

  • Risk of bias was generally unclear or high, and many trials did not report how they monitored block.
  • 'At least one adverse event' lumps dry mouth with desaturation.
  • I read the abstract, which gives no effect size for most individual events.
  • The search ended before SNaPP (June 2026, in this feed), where pulmonary complications or death were 19.0% vs 21.5%, a real but modest effect.

For us. Faster, more reliable reversal is now hard to dispute; a large patient-outcome benefit is less certain. Where the price gap has narrowed, sugammadex as default for aminosteroid block is easy to defend, especially in patients with little respiratory reserve. Quantitative monitoring still matters with either drug.

item.title: CLASP II TR: PASCAL tricuspid repair beat medical therapy, win ratio 1.98 at 6 months, driven mainly by quality of life
item.description:
TCT 2026 · Conference · 2026-11-02

This randomized trial assigned 450 patients with symptomatic severe or greater tricuspid regurgitation 2:1 to transcatheter repair with the PASCAL system plus optimal medical therapy or to medical therapy alone, at 58 North American sites. Results came as a late-breaker at TCT 2026, with no journal paper noted yet.

Take-home

  • PASCAL plus medical therapy beat medical therapy alone on the 6-month hierarchical win ratio: 1.98 (95% CI 1.47-2.67), driven largely by quality of life
  • At 1 year, 80% had moderate or less TR vs 30% of controls; KCCQ-OS difference was 10.9 points at 6 months
  • At 1 year, death was 8.8% vs 4.6% and HF hospitalization 13.2% vs 12.9%, neither significant; 30-day major adverse events were 6.9% with PASCAL

Why it matters. Edwards says FDA approved PASCAL for tricuspid repair in October 2026, so more of these cases may reach TEE and anesthesia teams. CLASP II TR is the randomized evidence behind that device.

What they did. Davidson, Arnold and colleagues randomized symptomatic patients with severe or greater TR, NYHA class II-IV and at least intermediate surgical risk. The primary endpoint was a hierarchy of death, RVAD or transplant, tricuspid surgery or intervention, HF hospitalization and KCCQ-OS. Over 40% had massive or torrential TR. The registry entry on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04097145) lists the same composite at 6 months.

What they found. PASCAL won 47.5% of comparisons and controls 24%. KCCQ-OS improved 17.5 vs 2.2 points at 30 days. Implant success was 92.5%, median procedure time 106 minutes and median stay 1 day. Single-leaflet attachment was 3.4% at 30 days, severe bleeding 3.1%.

Caveats.

  • The endpoint moved from 24 to 6 months because controls left after TriClip and Evoque were approved. Discussant Jörg Hausleiter asked what the result would have been otherwise.
  • The win came mostly from a patient-reported measure, with a medical-therapy control and no sham described; mortality was numerically higher with PASCAL, not significantly.
  • Edwards funded the trial, and these numbers come from congress coverage, not a paper.

For us. This is a fourth trial with the same message: tricuspid repair helps how patients feel, with hard-outcome questions open. Two-thirds here had CKD stage 3 or worse, and a quarter had an HF hospitalization in the prior year. Expect long leaflet-grasping imaging, and check for single-leaflet attachment before the case ends. Watch the RV as TR falls.

item.title: PROGRESS: TAVR beat surveillance in moderate AS with at-risk features: death or HF event 16.7% vs 23.9% at 2 years
item.description:
NEJM · RCT · 2026-11-02

An international open-label trial randomized 744 patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at least one at-risk feature to transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or to clinical surveillance. The primary end point was death from any cause or a heart-failure event at 2 years.

Take-home

  • In moderate AS with at-risk features, TAVR beat clinical surveillance for death or heart-failure event at 2 years: 16.7% vs 23.9% (P=0.02)
  • Heart-failure events drove the difference, 10.8% vs 19.0%; all-cause death was 8.4% with TAVR and 7.3% with surveillance
  • Procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between TAVR patients and surveillance patients who went on to valve replacement

Why it matters. Guidelines tell us to watch moderate aortic stenosis with echo every 1 or 2 years. PROGRESS asks whether treating selected patients early does better, and if it changes practice the structural list gets a new group of patients.

What they did. 744 patients (mean age 78, 39.1% women, 45.6% low surgical risk; mean valve area 1.2 cm², peak velocity 3.3 m/s) with at least one symptom or structural or functional abnormality were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral balloon-expandable TAVR or clinical surveillance. Surveillance patients could have valve replacement when indicated.

What they found.

  • Death or heart-failure event: 16.7% vs 23.9% (risk difference -7.2 points, 95% CI -13.1 to -1.3).
  • Heart-failure event: 10.8% vs 19.0%.
  • All-cause death: 8.4% vs 7.3%, so no survival gain at 2 years.

Caveats. Open-label and funded by Edwards, with a softer end point doing the work. Cedars-Sinai's release says more than half of the surveillance patients had valve replacement within 2 years, which blurs the comparison, and that follow-up continues to 10 years for durability and survival. Investigators there state plainly that this does not mean every moderate AS patient needs TAVR.

For the anesthesiologist. Expect older, comorbid patients with less severe gradients on the structural list; their risk may sit more in the ventricle and comorbidities than in the valve. Careful grading matters more now, so report valve area, velocity and the structural findings that may count as at-risk features. The trial says nothing about TAVR before noncardiac surgery or adding AVR during other cardiac surgery, so do not stretch it to those decisions.

item.title: Bicarbonate in ICU metabolic acidosis: no clear survival gain in 4 RCTs, but a 97% probability of fewer RRT initiations
item.description:
Intensive Care Med · Meta-analysis · 2026-11-02

A Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis pooled four randomized trials (1544 adults) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in ICU patients with metabolic acidosis. Short-term mortality was the primary outcome.

Take-home

  • Across four RCTs and 1544 patients, bicarbonate showed no clear short-term mortality benefit: RR 0.94 (95% CrI 0.73-1.22), probability of benefit 72.1%
  • Renal replacement therapy initiation was lower with bicarbonate: RR 0.74 (95% CrI 0.59-0.98), posterior probability of benefit 97.2%
  • Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise with no consistent safety signal; further trials should define who is most likely to benefit

Why it matters. Recent trials pulled in different directions: BICARICU-2 reported less dialysis, while SODa-BIC found no gain in kidney outcomes or death. This pooled analysis, searched through April 2026, gives a single estimate to set against those headlines.

What they did. A systematic review of MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL, with Bayesian random-effects pooling of RCTs of IV sodium bicarbonate against placebo or usual care in adult ICU patients with metabolic acidosis. The abstract does not name the four trials.

What they found.

  • Short-term mortality: RR 0.94 (95% CrI 0.73-1.22), a 72.1% probability of benefit.
  • RRT initiation: RR 0.74 (95% CrI 0.59-0.98), a 97.2% probability of benefit.
  • Other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal appeared.

Caveats. Only four trials, so the mortality interval still spans a meaningful benefit and meaningful harm. The decision to start RRT is made by clinicians and can follow the numbers on the gas, so a lower start rate is not automatically better kidney biology. We read the abstract only; it gives no pH thresholds or subgroup results.

For the anesthesiologist. This does not make bicarbonate routine for acidosis in the shocked patient, in the OR or the ICU. It does support considering it when the question is avoiding or delaying dialysis, with eyes open: it adds a sodium load and generates CO2 that your ventilation has to clear.

item.title: TRAVEL III: LuX-Valve Plus TTVR met a 6-month composite in 82.9% vs 4.8% on medical therapy alone in severe TR
item.description:
TCT 2026 · Conference · 2026-11-01

A randomized late-breaking trial at TCT 2026 compared transjugular tricuspid valve replacement plus optimal medical therapy with medical therapy alone in 126 high-risk patients with severe or greater tricuspid regurgitation.

Take-home

  • Transjugular LuX-Valve Plus TTVR plus OMT beat OMT alone: 6-month composite success 82.9% vs 4.8% (difference 78.1%, 95% CI 67.5-88.8; p<0.001).
  • 126 randomized patients with severe or greater TR, NYHA III-IV and high surgical risk; Ge calls it the first randomized evidence for this device.
  • TR fell in all TTVR patients, to moderate or less in 93%; no MI, stroke, access-site complication or device-related PE at 6 months.

Why it matters. Transcatheter tricuspid therapy is moving quickly, and this adds a randomized comparison for a jugular-delivered replacement valve. Ge describes it as the first randomized evidence for transjugular TTVR with this system.

What they did. Ge and colleagues randomized 126 patients with severe or greater TR, NYHA class III-IV and high surgical risk to LuX-Valve Plus plus optimal medical therapy or medical therapy alone. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07705594) lists 2:1 allocation, age 65 or older, and exclusions including LVEF below 50%, renal replacement therapy, MELD-albumin of 12 or more, and respiratory disease too severe for general anesthesia.

What they found. The six-month composite (alive, no HF rehospitalization, TR down at least one grade, NYHA up at least one class) was met by 82.9% vs 4.8%. TR fell in all treated patients, to moderate or less in 93%. No MI, stroke, access-site complication or device-related PE occurred by six months, and pacemaker rates were described as low.

Caveats. This is a congress report with no paper noted yet, and the ACC summary gives no figures for the 30-day major adverse event endpoint, mortality or pacemakers. The composite requires TR reduction, which medical therapy seldom achieves, plus NYHA class with no sham described, so a wide gap was close to built in. It is small, sponsor-run and followed for six months so far.

For us. Not practice-changing yet, and the report says nothing about anesthesia or imaging. Expect older patients with preserved LVEF and tired right ventricles; abolishing TR can load the RV abruptly, so watch RV function and conduction around deployment. A registered 680-patient pivotal trial lists LuX-Valve Plus and EVOQUE as interventions, so TEE teams may meet this device.

item.title: SEASON-AR: TAVR plus medical therapy cut 1-year death, disabling stroke or HF readmission to 8.3% vs 24.8% in pure AR
item.description:
Circulation · RCT · 2026-10-31

A multicenter open-label trial in China randomized 210 patients with severe pure aortic regurgitation, judged poor surgical candidates or declining surgery, to transfemoral TAVR with the self-expanding VitaFlow valve plus medical therapy or to medical therapy alone.

Take-home

  • TAVR plus GDMT lowered 1-year death, disabling stroke or heart failure rehospitalization: 8.3% vs 24.8% with GDMT alone (HR 0.31)
  • The benefit was driven mainly by fewer heart failure rehospitalizations, 3.7% vs 21.3% (HR 0.16)
  • TAVR carried higher rates of major or life-threatening bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation, mostly within 30 days

Why it matters. Pure aortic regurgitation has been the awkward case for TAVR: without annular calcium the frame has little to grip, and the pivotal TAVR trials excluded these patients. People too frail for surgery have usually been left on medical therapy alone. SEASON-AR is, by the authors' account, the first adequately powered randomized comparison of TAVR against guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in this group.

What they did. At 18 centers in China, 210 patients with severe pure AR whom the local heart team judged difficult or unacceptable surgical candidates, or who declined surgery, were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR with the self-expanding VitaFlow valve plus GDMT, or to GDMT alone. The primary end point was death, disabling stroke or heart failure rehospitalization at 1 year.

What they found.

  • Primary end point: 8.3% vs 24.8% (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.14-0.66).
  • The gap came mainly from heart failure rehospitalization: 3.7% vs 21.3% (HR 0.16).
  • TAVR brought more major or life-threatening bleeding and more new permanent pacemakers, mostly in the first 30 days.

Caveats. Open-label, so the softer rehospitalization end point is open to bias; one valve in one country; 1-year follow-up only; and the abstract does not report death or stroke separately.

For the anesthesiologist. Expect more of these cases on the structural list. With no calcium to anchor the valve, positioning is less forgiving: plan for migration or embolization and a possible second valve, keep pacing ready for new conduction block, and use echo to confirm position, grade paravalvular leak and watch for new wall-motion abnormalities. These are often dilated, volume-loaded ventricles, so avoid bradycardia and long diastoles until the valve is seated.

item.title: Global ACLF definition: liver failure (bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL, INR ≥1.5) plus dysfunction or failure of another organ
item.description:
Hepatology · Consensus · 2026-10-30

AASLD, EASL, APASL, ALEH and SOLDA used a Delphi process to merge the competing regional definitions of acute-on-chronic liver failure into one framework for diagnosis, grading, intensive care, transplant decisions and trial design. It appeared on the same day in Hepatology, Journal of Hepatology, Annals of Hepatology and Hepatology International.

Take-home

  • ACLF requires liver failure (bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL and INR ≥1.5) plus at least one extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure, in advanced chronic liver disease
  • Grades: 1, one extrahepatic organ dysfunction; 2, one organ failure; 3, two or more. Type B follows prior decompensation; type A does not
  • Organ failure: KDIGO AKI stage 2-3 or new RRT, West Haven grade 3-4 encephalopathy, vasopressors (not for HRS-AKI alone), or ventilation or PaO2/FiO2 ≤225

Why it matters. ACLF has meant different things in different places: Europe used the EASL-CLIF criteria, North America NACSELD and Asia APASL, so ICU triage, transplant prioritisation and trial results did not carry across borders. For anyone anaesthetising or ventilating a decompensated cirrhotic, the label should now mean the same thing everywhere.

What they did. Each of the five continental liver societies nominated chairs, members and young investigators. Statements needed more than 70% agreement in a Delphi process, with a second round after an open session before the EASL 2026 congress.

What it says.

  • Population: advanced chronic liver disease (fibrosis F3 or higher), not only cirrhosis; noninvasive tests alone should not establish it.
  • Liver failure (bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL and INR ≥1.5) is required.
  • Organ failures: KDIGO AKI stage 2-3 or starting kidney replacement therapy; West Haven grade 3-4 encephalopathy or ventilation for it; any vasopressor except for HRS-AKI alone; ventilation, PaO2/FiO2 ≤225, or SpO2/FiO2 ≤244 when no blood gas is available.
  • Dysfunction (grade 1), for example KDIGO stage 1 AKI or grade 2 encephalopathy; circulatory or respiratory dysfunction counts only in a monitored high-dependency or intensive care setting.
  • Transplant: offer it only when expected 1-year survival is above 75% to 80%. Listing should not be a trial's primary endpoint; survival with or without transplant between day 30 and month 6 could serve as a major one.

Caveats. We could read the abstract, the EASL release and HCPLive's report, not the full document, so the thresholds are as reported there.

For the anesthesiologist. Respiratory, circulatory and kidney failure are defined largely by the support we start. Intubating, starting a vasopressor or starting RRT can move a patient up a grade, and grade feeds transplant and prognosis decisions, so record why each support was started.

item.title: FDA Class I recall: four HemosIL AcuStar HIT-IgG assay lots read 20-35% low and can report HIT antibodies as negative
item.description:
FDA · Safety alert · 2026-10-30

Werfen (Instrumentation Laboratory) is removing four lots of its automated chemiluminescent PF4-heparin IgG antibody assay because of a negative bias that routine calibration and quality control may not catch. FDA posted the notice on October 30 and called it the most serious type of recall.

Take-home

  • Lots B38062, B38063, B40005 and B40006 show a 20-35% negative bias, so results can fall below the 1.00 U/mL cut-off
  • Routine calibration and QC may not detect the bias; a false-negative result may delay recognition of HIT while heparin continues
  • Destroy affected stock and line up another HIT antibody test, as a supply interruption is expected; no serious injuries or deaths reported

Why it matters. Cardiac surgery and ECMO patients are heavily exposed to heparin, and a negative PF4-heparin antibody immunoassay is often what lets a team keep heparin running or plan bypass with it. This recall covers lots of an automated assay that can read falsely negative.

What happened. Customers reported invalid calibration curves; one complaint showed a 47% negative mean bias with patient samples, and Werfen's investigation confirmed a 20-35% negative bias in four lots (part numbers 0009800127 and 0009802028; lots B38062 and B38063 expire 1 November 2026, B40005 and B40006 on 16 January 2027). The bias may slip past routine calibration and QC and push results below the 1.00 U/mL cut-off, so they are reported as HIT IgG antibody negative. FDA posted the notice on 30 October 2026 and classed it as the most serious type of recall. Health Canada had already recalled lot B38062 on 29 September.

What labs are told. Check stock, destroy the affected lots and record it on Werfen's tracking form, and arrange a replacement HIT antibody test because a supply interruption is expected. FDA leaves patient-level decisions to the laboratory and the treating clinician.

Caveats. As of September 3, Werfen had reported no serious injuries or deaths. The root cause is unknown. One sentence of the FDA notice says 'false positive negative', but the mechanism it describes, a low reading, produces false negatives.

For the anesthesiologist. Ask your lab whether it ran these lots and whether it is switching platforms. If a patient you still suspect of HIT had a negative result from them, do not let that result alone clear heparin for bypass or ECMO; ask the lab about repeat testing on another assay.

item.title: PROSpect: neither prone positioning nor HFOV added ventilator-free days in early moderate-to-severe pediatric ARDS
item.description:
Lancet · RCT · 2026-10-30

In 75 PICUs in 18 countries, 424 children with early moderate-to-severe PARDS were randomised in a two-by-two factorial design to prone or supine positioning and to HFOV or conventional ventilation. The trial stopped early for futility, and ventilator-free days to day 28 did not differ for either comparison.

Take-home

  • Ventilator-free days did not differ: prone 17.9 vs supine 17.4 days; HFOV 17.3 vs conventional ventilation 18.0 days
  • Proning brought more airway plugging (rate ratio 4.83) and pressure injuries (6% vs 1%); HFOV more haemodynamic instability (rate ratio 1.84)
  • The authors found no evidence for prone positioning or HFOV as first-line strategies and do not recommend their routine use

Why it matters. Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) are the rescue moves most PICUs reach for when a ventilated child's oxygenation worsens, yet practice varies because the pediatric data were inconclusive. Adult evidence pulls in opposite directions: proning cut mortality in severe ARDS (PROSEVA), while HFOV did not help (OSCILLATE, OSCAR).

What they did. This NHLBI-funded two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive trial in 75 PICUs across 18 countries enrolled patients aged 2 weeks to 20 years who had been intubated for less than 96 h before meeting moderate-to-severe PARDS criteria. Each was randomised to supine or prone and to conventional ventilation or HFOV. The primary outcome was ventilator-free days to day 28.

What they found.

  • Enrolment stopped at 424 of 600 planned patients, for futility and slow recruitment; 168 were allocated to the HFOV arms.
  • Ventilator-free days: prone 17.9 vs supine 17.4 (location shift 0.0, 95% CI -0.8 to 1.0); HFOV 17.3 vs conventional 18.0 (-0.3, -1.5 to 0.5).
  • 10% had died by day 28, with no group differences.
  • Proning brought more airway plugging (rate ratio 4.83) and stage 2 or worse pressure injuries (6% vs 1%); HFOV more haemodynamic instability (rate ratio 1.84).

Caveats. Unmasked and stopped early, but both confidence intervals exclude the 2-day gain the investigators registered as clinically meaningful.

For the anesthesiologist. We are often called to help prone a hypoxaemic child or move them to the oscillator. PROSpect says neither belongs as a routine first-line step in early moderate-to-severe PARDS; lung-protective conventional ventilation stays the base. If a child is proned, secure the tube and plan suctioning, since airway plugging rose almost five-fold. The registration excluded cyanotic heart disease and cardiomyopathy, so the trial does not speak to the post-bypass cardiac child.

item.title: Perioperative esketamine cut 3-month chronic pain after VATS lung resection, 14.7% vs 21.2%, in a 914-patient trial
item.description:
BJA · RCT · 2026-10-28

In a double-blind multicentre trial in China, 914 adults having video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection received esketamine (0.1 mg/kg at induction, 0.1 mg/kg/h during surgery, then 0.015 mg/kg/h for 48 h) or saline. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months.

Take-home

  • Chronic pain at 3 months (NRS 1 or more on coughing): 14.7% with esketamine vs 21.2% with saline; adjusted OR 0.62 (95% CI 0.43-0.90)
  • A post hoc threshold of NRS 3 or more on coughing also favoured esketamine (adjusted OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19-0.84)
  • Esketamine lowered pain at rest and on coughing over 48 h and reduced supplemental analgesic use, without increasing adverse effects

Why it matters. Persistent pain after lung resection remains common even with thoracoscopic surgery, and few preventive strategies have been tested in large blinded trials. This one tested a simple infusion in a thoracic population large enough to look at chronic pain as the primary outcome.

What they did. Adults having VATS lung resection were randomised 1:1 to esketamine or saline: a 0.1 mg/kg bolus at induction, 0.1 mg/kg/h during surgery and 0.015 mg/kg/h for 48 h afterwards. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months, defined as persistent pain in the surgical region scoring 1 or more on the numeric rating scale during coughing. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000040012).

What they found.

  • 873 of 914 randomised patients were analysed; median age 55, 63% female.
  • 3-month chronic pain: 14.7% vs 21.2% (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.90).
  • With a post hoc cut-off of NRS 3 or more on coughing: adjusted OR 0.39 (0.19-0.84).
  • Lower pain scores at rest and on coughing for 48 h and less supplemental analgesia through 48 h and 3 months, with no increase in adverse effects.

Caveats. The primary definition counts any pain on coughing, the moderate-pain analysis was post hoc, and the abstract reports outcomes only to 3 months. Intravenous esketamine is not marketed in the United States, so racemic ketamine would be the nearest substitute, and it was not what this trial tested.

For the anesthesiologist. For VATS lung resection, a low-dose esketamine infusion that continues for 48 h after surgery is a reasonable addition to multimodal analgesia where the drug is available. Note that the regimen ran into the postoperative period; an induction bolus alone is not what was studied.

item.title: NasoVISI: videolaryngoscopy beat direct laryngoscopy for infant nasotracheal intubation, 83% vs 75% first-pass success
item.description:
Lancet Child & Adolescent Health · RCT · 2026-10-27

Eight US pediatric cardiac centres randomised 684 infants aged 365 days or younger, without anticipated difficult airways, who needed nasotracheal intubation for elective cardiothoracic surgery or catheterisation, to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy. The primary outcome was first-attempt success.

Take-home

  • First-attempt success was 83% with videolaryngoscopy vs 75% with direct laryngoscopy; adjusted risk difference 8.2% (95% CI 2.0-14.3)
  • Complications were similar: 13% vs 12% on the first attempt and 14% in both groups across all attempts; no cardiac arrests or deaths
  • The authors say the result adds to growing evidence favouring videolaryngoscopy as the first-line technique for tracheal intubation in infants

Why it matters. Many pediatric cardiac centres intubate infants through the nose because a nasal tube is easier to secure for postoperative ventilation. Videolaryngoscopy already improves first-attempt success for oral intubation in infants, but its value for nasotracheal intubation, where the tube is steered from the nose, often with Magill forceps, had not been tested. NasoVISI, funded by the APSF and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, asked that question where nasal tubes are routine.

What they did. Eight US pediatric cardiac centres randomised infants aged 365 days or younger, without anticipated difficult airways, who needed nasotracheal intubation for elective cardiothoracic surgery or cardiac catheterisation, to a videolaryngoscope or standard direct laryngoscopy. First-attempt success was the primary outcome, analysed with models that accounted for clustering by intubating clinician.

What they found.

  • 673 of 684 randomised infants were analysed; median age 14 weeks, mean weight 4.8 kg.
  • First-attempt success: 83% vs 75% (adjusted risk difference 8.2%, 95% CI 2.0-14.3).
  • First-attempt complications 13% vs 12%; any complication across attempts 14% in each group; no cardiac arrest or death.

Caveats. These were elective cases at experienced cardiac centres. The registration excluded infants under 2 kg or under 36 weeks' gestation and any infant with a known or predicted difficult airway, and the authors list difficult airways, non-specialist centres and urgent settings as open questions.

For the anesthesiologist. For an infant coming to the cardiac room with a planned nasal tube, starting with the videolaryngoscope gives about one extra first-pass success for every 12 infants intubated. Complications did not fall, so the gain is in first-pass success rather than proven safety. For the very small, the premature and the anticipated difficult airway, the trial offers no answer yet.

item.title: HFSA: right heart failure is its own syndrome; acute care must address preload, RV afterload and contractility together
item.description:
J Card Fail · Consensus · 2026-10-27

The Heart Failure Society of America published a scientific statement in the Journal of Cardiac Failure that frames right heart failure as a distinct clinical syndrome, with ten take-home messages on diagnosis, acute care, PAH drugs, temporary MCS and the timing of tricuspid intervention.

Take-home

  • Acute RHF needs all three pillars at once: optimize preload, reduce RV afterload, support contractility and perfusion, plus rhythm control and RV-protective ventilation
  • After LVAD or heart transplant, standardized perioperative management of preload, pulmonary vascular load, contractility and rhythm may enable earlier recognition
  • Temporary MCS (percutaneous or surgical RVAD, VA-ECMO) may be considered for refractory RHF with shock; choose by physiology, oxygenation needs and destination

Why it matters. Right ventricular failure is among the hardest problems in cardiac anesthesia, off bypass, at LVAD implantation and after transplant, yet it is often treated as a by-product of left heart disease. HFSA now calls it common, prognostically important across heart failure, and a distinct clinical syndrome.

What they did. Corresponding author Manreet Kanwar (University of Chicago) and senior author Ryan Tedford (Medical University of South Carolina) published the statement in the Journal of Cardiac Failure on 27 October 2026, with ten take-home messages.

What they say.

  • No single measurement defines RHF: combine examination, biomarkers and echo, adding right-heart catheterization when precision is needed.
  • Acute RHF: optimize preload, reduce RV afterload and support contractility and systemic perfusion simultaneously, with rhythm management and RV-protective ventilation.
  • After LVAD or transplant, standardized perioperative management of preload, pulmonary vascular load, contractility and rhythm may speed recognition and treatment.
  • PAH-targeted drugs help properly classified PAH but should not be used routinely in pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, where trials mostly showed no benefit and some agents caused edema or harm; hemodynamic phenotyping comes first.
  • Temporary MCS (percutaneous RVADs, surgical RVADs, VA-ECMO) may be considered for refractory RHF with cardiogenic shock, chosen by dominant physiology, oxygenation needs and destination.
  • Consider surgical or transcatheter tricuspid intervention before RV dysfunction is advanced.

Caveats. We read the HFSA press release, not the full statement; it gives no staging system or numeric cut-offs, and the authors list consensus definitions as a research need.

For the anesthesiologist. The three pillars are the levers we already pull after bypass or at LVAD implantation: volume, pulmonary vasodilation with RV-sparing ventilation, inotropes and rhythm. Judge the RV on TEE with several measures, not one number, and decide early who needs a right-sided device.

item.title: ESICM consensus on human-centred ICU care: flexible family visiting, structured team communication, staff support too
item.description:
Intensive Care Med · Consensus · 2026-10-26

An international ESICM panel of 46 ran rapid reviews on 20 PICO questions across six domains, put 53 draft statements through a two-round eDelphi (201, then 149 stakeholders) and ratified 43 at a consensus meeting with patient and family representatives.

Take-home

  • Key recommendations support flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication and empathy-based training for ICU staff.
  • Psychological support should reach both patients and ICU professionals, together with culturally responsive care.
  • Environmental measures to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and integration of digital technologies, complete a 43-statement framework for diverse ICU settings.

Why it matters. ICU care is no longer judged on survival alone: how families are included, how the team communicates and how staff cope all shape delirium, recovery after discharge and burnout. ESICM has now put a formal consensus behind practices that many units apply unevenly, from open visiting to structured family updates.

What they did. A 46-member international, multidisciplinary panel ran rapid reviews on 20 PICO questions in six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity and inclusion; the ICU environment; and technology and innovation. Of 53 draft statements, a two-round eDelphi (201 participants in round 1, 149 in round 2) and a consensus meeting that included patient and family representatives endorsed 43.

What they recommend (from the abstract):

  • Flexible family visitation
  • Structured interdisciplinary communication
  • Empathy-based training for staff
  • Psychological support for patients and for ICU professionals
  • Culturally responsive care
  • Environmental measures to improve sleep and reduce delirium
  • Integration of digital technologies

Caveats. This is a Delphi consensus built on rapid reviews rather than a graded guideline, so the statements record agreement, not proven effects on hard outcomes. We read the abstract only; the full document gives the exact wording of each statement and the level of agreement behind it.

For the anesthesiologist. If you staff a cardiothoracic or surgical ICU, this is an ESICM-backed reference for local policy: open visiting after cardiac surgery, a fixed structure for family updates and handovers, night-time noise and light rules as part of delirium prevention, and debriefing or psychological support for the team after hard cases.

item.title: PROSPECT shoulder replacement: single-shot interscalene, paracetamol, NSAID, dexamethasone; not liposomal bupivacaine
item.description:
Anaesthesia · Guideline · 2026-10-22

A systematic review using PROSPECT methodology identified 1,809 articles, included 30 randomised trials and seven systematic reviews, and produced procedure-specific pain management recommendations for total shoulder arthroplasty.

Take-home

  • Basic regimen: paracetamol, an NSAID started peri-operatively and continued afterwards, IV dexamethasone 8-10 mg, and opioids only for rescue.
  • Regional: single-bolus interscalene block with bupivacaine or ropivacaine, not liposomal bupivacaine; local infiltration analgesia if contraindicated or expertise is lacking.
  • Evidence was conflicting for continuous interscalene catheters and for liposomal bupivacaine, and no evidence favoured a specific surgical technique.

Why it matters. Total shoulder arthroplasty causes moderate-to-severe pain, and the analgesic menu varies a lot between centres: single-shot or catheter interscalene, liposomal bupivacaine, surgeon-delivered infiltration. PROSPECT recommendations are a widely used procedure-specific reference for enhanced-recovery pathways.

What they did. A systematic review using PROSPECT methodology of English-language randomised trials and systematic reviews that measured postoperative pain after analgesic, anaesthetic or surgical interventions. Of 1,809 articles identified, 30 randomised trials and seven systematic reviews or meta-analyses were included, and the findings were turned into PROSPECT recommendations.

What they recommend.

  • Paracetamol plus an NSAID given peri-operatively and continued after surgery.
  • IV dexamethasone 8-10 mg.
  • Single-bolus interscalene brachial plexus block with a long-acting local anaesthetic (bupivacaine or ropivacaine), not liposomal bupivacaine.
  • Local infiltration analgesia when the block is contraindicated or the expertise is not available.
  • Opioids for rescue only.

Caveats. Evidence on continuous interscalene catheters and on liposomal bupivacaine was conflicting, and the authors call for more trials of continuous infusions. The abstract does not say how diaphragm-sparing options such as superior trunk or suprascapular-based blocks were judged, so read the full paper before rebuilding a pathway around them.

What it means for us. The default for a shoulder arthroplasty list is simple and cheap: paracetamol, NSAID, 8-10 mg dexamethasone and a single-shot interscalene with plain bupivacaine or ropivacaine. When the interscalene is a poor choice, for example in a patient with little respiratory reserve, the recommended fallback is infiltration analgesia. Because the catheter question is still open, plan multimodal cover for the night the block wears off.

item.title: STS borderline left heart consensus: stage LV recruitment in grey-zone neonates rather than primary biventricular repair
item.description:
Ann Thorac Surg · Consensus · 2026-10-20

An STS panel of congenital surgeons, cardiologists and imagers used PICO questions, literature searches and a modified Delphi process to write consensus statements on borderline left heart in the first year of life, excluding unbalanced AVSD.

Take-home

  • Primary biventricular repair in neonates with borderline left heart should be adopted cautiously, only with favorable anatomic and physiologic criteria on echo and/or MRI.
  • Grey-zone neonates (small mitral and aortic valves, endocardial fibroelastosis, small LV) should undergo staged recruitment to encourage left-sided growth.
  • Initial palliation can be surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1; interval catheterization and MRI should guide timing of later biventricular conversion.

Why it matters: Whether a small left heart can carry a biventricular circulation is one of the hardest calls in congenital cardiac surgery, and practice varies widely between centers. This is the first STS expert consensus to put structure around it, and it shapes which operations (and anesthetics) these infants will need over their first year.

What they did: An STS panel of congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists and imaging experts framed key management questions with the PICO approach, searched the literature for each, and built consensus statements with a modified Delphi method. Scope: borderline left heart from the neonatal period through 1 year, excluding unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect.

What they recommend:

  • Primary biventricular repair only for neonates with clearly favorable anatomy and physiology on echo and/or MRI.
  • For the 'grey zone' (smaller mitral and aortic valves, endocardial fibroelastosis, small indexed LV diastolic volume, low ascending aortic flow): staged LV recruitment.
  • Initial palliation by surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1, possibly with atrial-level restriction; later EFE resection plus mitral and aortic valve repair as parts of complete biventricular conversion.
  • Interval catheterization and MRI to time later steps.

Caveats: This is expert consensus built on a thin, mostly observational evidence base; the specific numeric thresholds are in the full document and were not legible in the abstract we read.

For the anesthesiologist: Expect more hybrid stage 1 and staged recruitment pathways, which means repeated anesthetics for catheterization and MRI in fragile single-ventricle-physiology infants, and a central role for TEE in judging mitral and aortic inflow, LV size and EFE at each surgical step.

item.title: FDA approves cipepofol (Cypsedo), a new IV agent for induction in adults; launch waits on DEA scheduling
item.description:
FDA · FDA/Regulatory · 2026-05-29

FDA approved Haisco's Cypsedo (cipepofol) injection, 50 mg/20 mL, for induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery. The approval letter says it cannot be marketed until DEA schedules cipepofol and the label is updated.

Take-home

  • Approved indication: induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery; cipepofol injection 50 mg/20 mL (NDA 220482, approval letter May 29, 2026).
  • Marketing may begin only after DEA publishes an interim final scheduling notice for cipepofol and the labeling is revised to reflect scheduling.
  • Not approved in children: FDA required deferred pediatric trials, ages 3 to under 17 (report due 2028) and birth to under 3 (due 2030).

Why it matters. US anesthesiologists get a new intravenous induction agent alongside propofol, etomidate and ketamine. Cipepofol (Cypsedo, Haisco) has been reported as the first China-developed IV anesthetic approved for the US market.

What FDA approved. Cypsedo (cipepofol) injection, 50 mg in 20 mL (2.5 mg/mL) single-dose vials, for induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery (NDA 220482, letter signed May 29, 2026). Maintenance of anesthesia and procedural sedation are not part of the indication.

The catch: scheduling. The approval letter says marketing can start only after DEA publishes an interim final rule scheduling cipepofol and the label is revised to show it. Unlike propofol, it will arrive as a controlled substance, with the storage, wastage and documentation that implies.

Label highlights. The most common adverse reactions (2% or more) include injection-site pain and hypotension; procedural hypotension, hypertension and bradycardia are also listed. Warnings cover anaphylaxis, cardiorespiratory depression and additive hemodynamic effects with opioids and other sedatives, and patients with prior anaphylaxis to eggs, egg products, soybeans or soy products should not receive it. It is not approved in children; FDA required pediatric trials running to 2030.

What it means for us. Nothing changes until DEA acts. When it launches, read the label's dosing and hemodynamic data before using it in frail or cardiac patients, and decide early with pharmacy how a scheduled induction agent will be stocked and wasted.

item.title: FDA Class I: BD Alaris pump infusion sets perform worse than disclosed below 1 mL/h and with boluses of 5 mL or less
item.description:
FDA · Safety alert · 2026-10-05

FDA has updated its Class I recall of BD Alaris Pump Module (Model 8100) infusion sets after BD's August 2026 letter reported that sets with restrictive components perform worse than the 2025 field action disclosed. Under- or over-infusion, delayed occlusion alarms and inaccurate boluses are possible and may be hard to detect.

Take-home

  • Sets with closed male luers, filters, check valves, Y-sites or microbore tubing perform worse than previously disclosed.
  • Problems are most common at programmed rates under 1 mL/h and bolus volumes of 5 mL or less.
  • Discard discontinued sets, prioritize alternates for critical care, neonatal and pediatric units, or move to a syringe pump.

Why it matters. Alaris is the workhorse large-volume pump in many US hospitals, and this notice is about the infusions we care about most: vasopressors, inotropes and sedatives at a few tenths of a millilitre per hour, and small boluses. BD and CareFusion 303 recalled these sets in September 2025 (field action MMS-25-5311). Their August 19, 2026 letter replaces that information: updated testing found the earlier performance claims were overestimated and some sets perform significantly worse. FDA posted the updated notice on October 5, 2026 as a Class I recall.

What is affected. Alaris Pump Infusion Sets used with the Pump Module Model 8100 on Guardrails Suite MX software up to version 12.6, specifically sets with restrictive components: closed male luers, in-line filters, check valves, Y-sites and microbore tubing. Effects: under- or over-infusion, delayed occlusion alarms and bolus inaccuracies, mostly at rates under 1 mL/h and boluses of 5 mL or less, which users may not easily detect. Neonates, children and critically ill patients are the groups flagged. As of August 19, 2026, BD had reported no serious injuries or deaths.

What FDA asks. Discard the discontinued sets (Attachment C) and substitute appropriate alternates, prioritizing scarce ones for critical care, neonatal and pediatric areas; review the performance data in Attachment B; move to a syringe pump such as the Alaris Syringe Module where performance is not acceptable; otherwise use the recalled sets only with enhanced monitoring and the user-manual mitigations, including not hanging bags more than 21 inches above the pump.

Bedside take. Low-rate vasoactive infusions in cardiac surgical and ICU patients belong on syringe pumps with a carrier line. Ask pharmacy and biomed which set codes your ORs stock, and treat an unexplained haemodynamic swing on a low-rate Alaris infusion as a possible delivery problem before changing the dose.

item.title: AHA statement maps aortic surgery from the surgeon's, anesthesiologist's and perfusionist's seats and where they collide
item.description:
Circulation · Consensus · 2026-10-22

An American Heart Association scientific statement, written by cardiac surgeons and cardiac anesthesiologists, walks through the aortic surgery patient from each of the three intraoperative roles and the specific concerns each brings.

Take-home

  • Surgeons, anesthesiologists and perfusionists each act independently during cardiac surgery, yet one member's action can immediately affect the others.
  • Aortic surgery adds layers: single-lung ventilation, systemic cooling and rewarming, and myocardial, cerebral and visceral protection.
  • The statement presents each role's perspective to highlight specific concerns, and is explicitly not an exhaustive review of techniques.

Why it matters. Aortic operations are where the cardiac OR team is most interdependent: the surgeon picks the cannulation site and the perfusion strategy, the perfusionist runs cooling, rewarming and cerebral perfusion, and the anesthesiologist manages lung isolation, neuromonitoring, coagulation and TEE. A decision made in one seat changes the physiology the other two are managing, often within seconds.

What it is. A scientific statement from the AHA Council on Cardiovascular Surgery and Anesthesia, written by a mixed surgeon-anesthesiologist group (DeAnda, Steppan, Boskovski, Cherry, Dickey, DeAngelis, Ibekwe, Tseng). Rather than grading evidence, it takes the aortic surgery patient through the surgeon's, the anesthesiologist's and the perfusionist's perspectives and names the concerns each brings to the room.

What it covers (from the abstract):

  • The independent but coupled actions of the three disciplines during cardiac surgery
  • The extra demands of aortic work: one-lung ventilation for descending and thoracoabdominal repairs, deliberate cooling and rewarming, and protection of the heart, brain and viscera
  • How each role's priorities can align or conflict

Caveats. This is a perspective-style statement, not a graded guideline, and the authors say up front it is not an exhaustive review of techniques. We read the abstract only; check the full text for any specific recommendations.

For the anesthesiologist. A useful document to hand to trainees and to bring to a team debrief or a protocol meeting. It gives you shared language for the pre-incision huddle on aortic cases: cannulation and arterial line sites, neuromonitoring plan, temperature targets and rewarming rate, the cerebral perfusion strategy, and who calls what during circulatory arrest.

item.title: ESC consensus gives non-transplant clinicians a playbook for heart transplant recipients, noncardiac surgery included
item.description:
Eur J Heart Fail · Consensus · 2026-10-19

The Heart Failure Association and ACNAP of the ESC issued a clinical consensus statement on caring for heart transplant recipients outside transplant centres, covering immunosuppression, rejection, infection, late complications and situations such as noncardiac surgery.

Take-home

  • Better post-transplant survival means more long-term heart transplant recipients are now seen by clinicians outside specialised transplant centres.
  • The statement gives a structured framework: care by time since transplant, immunosuppression and drug monitoring, recognising rejection, and infection prophylaxis and treatment.
  • It covers noncardiac surgery, pregnancy, rehabilitation and palliative care, and stresses shared care with the centre and early referral.

Why it matters. Heart transplant recipients now live long enough to need hip replacements, cholecystectomies, cancer surgery and emergency trauma care, and most of that happens far from the transplant centre. The anesthesiologist covering that case is often the first clinician in days to think hard about the denervated heart, tacrolimus levels and infection risk.

What it is. A clinical consensus statement from the ESC's Heart Failure Association and its nursing and allied professions association (ACNAP), first author Baudry, written for non-transplant cardiologists, GPs and other clinicians with little post-transplant experience.

What it covers (from the abstract):

  • Care principles by time since transplant
  • Immunosuppressive therapy and therapeutic drug monitoring
  • Recognising and managing early rejection
  • Infection prophylaxis and treatment
  • Surveillance for cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, chronic kidney disease and metabolic disease
  • Special situations: fertility and pregnancy, noncardiac surgery, rehabilitation, palliative care
  • Shared-care models and the scenarios that need early referral back to the centre

Caveats. Consensus, not graded evidence, and we have read only the abstract, so the specific perioperative advice still needs checking in the full text.

For the anesthesiologist. Worth a bookmark for the next transplant recipient on an elective list. The usual perioperative checklist applies: call the transplant team before surgery, keep immunosuppression going with minimal interruption (and check levels when absorption or drug interactions change), think about stress-dose steroids, use strict asepsis for lines, protect the kidneys, and remember the denervated heart ignores atropine, so reach for direct-acting agents such as epinephrine or isoproterenol.
